mcqs.question: An algorithm sorts an n-element array by copying it into a new list and sorting the copy. When someone says its space complexity is 'O(n)' without qualification, what do they almost always mean?
options: O(n) auxiliary space — the extra copy the algorithm allocates, not counting the original input
O(n) total space, always including the input array
O(n) time, mislabeled as space
O(n) space per element of the input, which is a nonstandard phrasing
mcqs.explanation: By interview convention, an unqualified space-complexity claim means auxiliary space — the extra memory the algorithm itself allocates beyond the given input, since the input has to be stored somewhere regardless of algorithm choice. Here that's the O(n) copy; the input array isn't counted toward it.

mcqs.question: For a recursive function's space complexity, which quantity actually matters?
options: The total number of recursive calls made across the entire run
The number of base cases the function defines
The maximum number of stack frames alive at the same time — the deepest point in the recursion
The number of parameters passed to each call
mcqs.explanation: Space is about how many frames are simultaneously live, which is the recursion's maximum depth, not how many calls happened in total over the whole run — those are the numbers relevant to time, not space, and conflating them is the most common space-complexity mistake with recursive code.

mcqs.question: An iterative sum and a recursive sum over the same n-element list both run in O(n) time. Why can their space complexity differ?
options: It can't differ — same time complexity always means same space complexity
The recursive version must allocate an explicit array to track its progress
The iterative version secretly uses more memory due to loop overhead
The recursive version keeps one stack frame alive per unreturned call, reaching O(n) frames at max depth, while the loop reuses a single frame throughout
mcqs.explanation: Time and space are independent axes — the recursive version's n live stack frames at maximum depth cost O(n) space even though no explicit data structure is allocated, while the loop's single reused frame and accumulator variable keep space at O(1). Nothing here requires the recursive version to declare any array.

mcqs.question: A recursive function has no arrays, lists, or dicts declared anywhere in its body. Is it necessarily O(1) space?
options: No — each unreturned recursive call still holds a stack frame, so depth-n recursion is O(n) space regardless of visible variables
Yes, since space complexity only counts explicitly declared data structures
Yes, as long as the function has a single base case
No, but only if the function also takes an array as a parameter
mcqs.explanation: The absence of a visible data structure doesn't mean the absence of memory use — every unreturned call adds a stack frame, and depth-n recursion means n such frames alive simultaneously, which is O(n) space regardless of what variables the function body happens to declare.

mcqs.question: A function's recursive call is in tail position (the last operation before returning). Does this guarantee O(1) stack space in Python?
options: Yes, tail position always guarantees constant stack space in any language
Yes, because tail calls never allocate a new frame by definition
No — Python does not implement tail-call optimization, so a tail-recursive function still pushes a full frame per call and can still stack-overflow at depth
No, because Python forbids tail-recursive functions entirely
mcqs.explanation: Tail-call optimization is a compiler/runtime feature that Python (along with most JavaScript engines and standard Java) does not implement, so being in tail position doesn't change how the runtime actually behaves — a frame is still pushed per call, and deep tail recursion can still overflow the stack in these languages.

mcqs.question: Naive recursive Fibonacci makes O(2ⁿ) total calls across its whole run. What is its space complexity?
options: O(2ⁿ), matching its time complexity
O(n²), since the tree has that many total nodes at each level combined
O(1), since Fibonacci has no arrays
O(n) — only one root-to-leaf path is ever live on the stack at a time, regardless of the total call count
mcqs.explanation: Space depends on the tree's height (how deep one active path goes), not its total node count — at any instant only one root-to-leaf chain of calls is unreturned, giving O(n) stack space even though the total call count across the whole exponential tree is O(2ⁿ). Time comes from the whole tree; space comes from its height.
